1.summary: Lindsey Stirling - The Snow Waltz Tour
1.description: Lindsey Stirling brings her spectacular Snow Waltz Tour to State Farm Center this holiday season. The award-winning violinist, dancer and entertainer delivers a one-of-a-kind holiday experience featuring breathtaking choreography, stunning visuals and Lindsey’s genre-defying arrangements of holiday classics and original music. Blending classical violin with electronic, pop and rock influences, Stirling has created a live show unlike anything else — combining virtuosic musicianship with dance, theatrical production and aerial performance. Her annual holiday tour has become a seasonal tradition, bringing the music of her acclaimed Christmas albums Warmer in the Winter and Snow Waltz to life on stage. $1 per ticket goes towards Lindsey’s foundation, The Upside Fund, which focuses on equitable healthcare and medical debt relief, mental health access, and nutrition education and food justice.   Learn more about Lindsey Stirling - The Snow Waltz Tour

30.description: Maizy and Beau are getting hitched, when the corn that protects their small community starts to die. The town needs answers. It also celebrates and showcases the Rare Book & Manuscript Library’s recent acquisition of a first edition copy of the novel, made possible by a generous gift from Lionelle and Jim Elsesser, along with funds from several other endowments. Read more about the exhibit here.
58.location: Main Library Room 346 — 1408 W. Gregory Dr, Urbana, IL 61801

229.summary: \"These Plots Are Older Than We Are\": Celebrating the 150th Anniversary of the Morrow Plots
229.description: 'These Plots Are Older Than We Are’: Celebrating the 150th Anniversary of the Morrow Plots” is now on display in room 220 of the Main Library! The exhibit features a selection of materials primarily from the University Archives that document the Morrow Plots, spanning the experiment's establishment in 1876 to today, including photos, newspaper clippings, letters, data records, and more. These materials highlight the multifaceted scientific and cultural history of the Morrow Plots, the world’s oldest crop rotation study and the second-oldest continuous agricultural study. The exhibit is on display through November 30. Make sure to pick up a Morrow Plots zine when you're there!

234.summary: Exhibition | Ink Shower: Contemporary Taiwanese Artists Reimagine Tradition
234.description: For more than a thousand years, ink painting has been a venerable practice, conveying people’s deepest beliefs and highest aspirations. Ink art has expressed complex, evolving ideas about aesthetics, spirituality, and the nature of the human condition. In today’s world, the range of visual and cultural concerns at the heart of ink art—developed into a major artistic tradition in China during the Tang dynasty (618–907)—now informs a wide range of art, including painting, sculpture, video, photography, animation, and more. Ink Shower focuses on dynamic works of art in this vein produced by twelve Taiwanese artists. While the cultural fabric of Taiwan has been shaped by waves of colonialism, modernization, and globalization, the tradition of ink art in Taiwan has never been a mere continuation of history. Instead, it has evolved through a process of cultural bricolage—appropriating and transforming elements to create new meanings. Rooted in the genealogy of Chinese ink traditions, ink art in Taiwan has been deeply intertwined with local artistic developments since the mid-twentieth century. Over time, the singular path of “ink as tradition” has been gradually dismantled through movements such as modern ink painting, nativist realism, and conceptual art. Taiwanese artists have come to regard ink not merely as a medium, but as a conceptual device and cultural signifier—shifting from medium to spirit, and from spirit to a renewed engagement with diverse media. Ink Shower does not assert a direct narrative. Rather, it adopts an oblique, mobile, and peripheral strategy—entering from the margins, unfolding from dim light, and transforming “ink” into a cultural tool for understanding identity, reimagining history, and envisioning the future. 353.summary: Nutrition for Cats: Rethinking the Basics
353.description: Nutrition for Cats: Rethinking the Basics  We are pleased to invite you to a free live webinar featuring Dr. Mariana Fragoso Rentas.  Date: Tuesday, December 1, 2026  Time: 3:00 – 4:00 PM CT Format: Live Online Webinar     Dr. Mariana Fragoso Rentas is a Brazilian veterinarian, professor, researcher, and specialist in companion animal nutrition. She earned her DVM, Master’s, and PhD in Animal Nutrition and Production from the School of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Science of the University of São Paulo (FMVZ-USP), with a strong focus on companion animal nutrition. Her professional experience spans clinical nutrition, small animal medicine, university teaching, scientific research, and technical training in the pet food industry. She currently serves as a university professor in Brazil and is the Director of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital at UNINTA Fortaleza. Cats have unique nutritional requirements that are often misunderstood or oversimplified. In this session, Dr. Rentas will revisit the foundations of feline nutrition, discuss common misconceptions, and examine how modern research is influencing approaches to long-term feline health and wellbeing. Sign up for the mailing list to receive the webinar link and updates.https://go.illinois.edu/ipets-webinars

354.summary: Exploring the Deep, High-Cadence Sky with the Argus Array
354.description: The under-construction Argus Array will be the first large telescope able to observe the entire accessible sky simultaneously. Argus multiplexes 1200 optical telescopes to form a 122-gigapixel, 8m-class survey system capable of producing terabits per second of imaging data. Each one-minute, 8,000-square-degree Argus exposure will reach 20th magnitude across the Northern sky; deep imaging coadds will push far deeper; and GPU-based data pipelines will provide realtime image subtraction and transient source detection.  Argus will record more than 100,000 epochs per year everywhere in the Northern sky, following up multimessenger triggers within minutes, monitoring 100 million stars for planet-induced microlensing events, occultations, stellar flares and other variability, and performing dozens of other surveys with data that will be made public on extremely rapid timescales. I will discuss Argus's science, technical and data-release plans.

You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty.11:00am-11:45am: Kimberly Mack, CAS Associate 2025-26, English During her appointment as a CAS Associate, Kimberly Mack made considerable progress on a proposal and sample chapters for her critical memoir, Brown Sugar Blues: The White Soundtrack of a Black Girl Who Loves Rock. Brown Sugar Blues tells the story of how rock music both empowered and alienated Mack while growing up in a violent and musical home. It braids memoir, biography, and cultural criticism together to explore the personal and historical impacts of the erasure of Black people from rock—a style of music with Black origins. In this lecture, Mack considers the reasons and costs of Black women’s erasure from rock through the analysis of a controversial song that engages Black women and race, sex, power, and violence more directly than perhaps any other 1970s-era rock tune: “Brown Sugar” by the Rolling Stones. She tells the story of her mom’s uncritical love of the song, as well as her unwitting participation in her mom’s fandom, as a toddler, in 1971. Alongside this conversation about “Brown Sugar” is the story of how rock music helped Mack to bond with her mom while it simultaneously, due to its sexism and racism, complicated her budding awareness of her sexuality as a young Black girl. Noon-12:45pm: Laura Hetrick, CAS Associate 2025-26, Art + Design Beyond Voice: Reclaiming Neurodivergent Subjectivity as Knowers, Storytellers, and Scholars During a recent Center for Advanced Study appointment, Laura Hetrick completed drafts of two book-length projects that center neurodivergent voices and experiences. 381.summary: 'How (not) to Kill a Language: The Many Lives of Sumerian'
381.description: The Sumerian language has lived many lives. It first lived more than 5,000 years ago on the streets and in the homes of the people of modern day Iraq. Sumerian experienced a new way of living when it became the subject of writing, when the language was used to record not only how much beer moved from one place to another, but eventually the legends of kings, the praise of goddesses, the recipes to recovering health, and the lullabies of a mother. But eventually, Sumerian suffered from time and political shifts; its speakers ceased teaching their children. But in its dying breath, Sumerian was given a new life, a new purpose: the language was resuscitated as the language of an ancient past, the language taught to the schoolchildren who might one day wield power, the language used to create histories and shape ideas. It became a language of access: to culture, to power, to the gods. And even long after it finally breathed its last 2,000 years ago as its life support — writing — finally gave out, it was once again reincarnated through Victorian decipherment and modern academics and fantasy storytellers. In her recent book How to Kill a Language, the journalist Sophia Smith Galer tells the stories of languages killed through neglect, premeditation, and abuse. The story of Sumerian is a different story; a story of how a language breathes when afforded new lives.

405.summary: Saturday Physics for Everyone: Looking Inside the Hottest Matter in the Universe with Jets at the Large Hadron Collider
405.description: The matter around us is made up of atoms. Most of the material in an atom is in the nucleus at its core. The nucleus is made up of protons and neutrons. It turns out that protons and neutrons are in turn made up of quarks and gluons. It takes enormous energy to free these quarks and gluons. To do that we use the Large Hadron Collider (the LHC), a 17 mile ring 100 meters underneath Switzerland. Using the LHC, nuclei are accelerated to nearly the speed of light and smashed into each other. The resulting collision creates matter so hot that it melts the protons and neutrons inside the nuclei making a plasma of quarks and gluons. This matter lives for less than a billionth of a trillionth of a second and is trillions of degrees hot. In this talk, I'll discuss why we do this and what we've learned from these experiments. Saturday Physics for Everyone is an event series focused on sharing the research of the Department of Physics with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign community. High school students interested in STEM are highly encouraged to attend.

427.summary: Food For Thought | Tess McNulty and Alex Shakar
427.description: Food for Thought: A series of public events featuring research and creative projects by recent CAS Associates and Fellows. We are delighted to showcase the work of some of our most productive and creative faculty in this informal series of intellectually and spiritually invigorating presentations. You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty.11:00am-11:45am: Tess McNulty, CAS Fellow 2025-26, English  Content Culture: The Forms of the Viral Era For almost two decades, we’ve been living in the era of viral content, from listicles to AI slop. But while much academic work has addressed this new media as information (conveying facts) or communication (coalescing communities), far less has considered its operations as imaginative, aestheticized entertainment. In this talk, Professor McNulty presents work from a book project that provides the first overarching cultural history of viral content from an aesthetic perspective, defining what she calls this new media's five major genres and interpreting the significance of their ubiquity. Noon-12:45pm: Alex Shakar, CAS Associate 2019-20, English Play the Void, a novel A mutant mushroom virus has jumped tracks to spark a human pandemic. A fateful presidential election looms. And the legendary singer Vic Vibes has been found dead. Now, an uncanny impersonator, Vic Voids, leads a chameleonic music tour across the land. Its mission: “unite the vibes” by playing to all sides of an increasingly violent culture war and topping one musical chart after another. But who’s behind the tour and to what ends? Why is a trove of Vic’s secrets pouring out: a tale shadowed by a crime, a love, and a nation’s troubled history? And who—or what—is Voids? In this talk, Professor Shakar will read from and discuss his forthcoming novel.

429.summary: Creating authentic, AI-powered emerging technology with and for deaf signing students
429.description: Emerging technologies, including artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), and augmented reality (AR), offer new opportunities to create accessible, engaging, and effective learning experiences for deaf signing students and sign language learners. But how can we ensure that these technologies are grounded in research on learning and cognition, while also reflecting the linguistic and educational needs of deaf learners? In this talk, Dr. Lorna Quandt (Gallaudet University) will highlight three research projects that approach this challenge from complementary perspectives.Lorna Quandt, Ph.D., is a cognitive neuroscientist and professor of educational neuroscience at Gallaudet University. Her work advances accessible technology through research on sign language, perception, and learning. She leads interdisciplinary teams that develop and evaluate signing avatars, virtual and augmented reality learning environments, and technologies that support deaf and hard-of-hearing users. Combining experimental neuroscience with human–computer interaction, she examines how people perceive, understand, and learn from emerging technologies. She co-directs the Visual Language and Visual Learning Research Center and serves as science director of Motion Light Lab, emphasizing equitable collaboration and research grounded in deaf people’s language, experiences, and priorities.

435.summary: Planetary Architectures and Insights Towards Planet Formation
435.description: After a brief discussion about the types of exoplanetary architectures discovered so far, I will focus on one sub-population and what we can learn about planet formation by studying it in depth. Hot Jupiters were long thought to be lonely planets. This correctly describes the majority of the population and strongly motivates high-eccentricity tidal migration as the most common method of taking a hot Jupiter to its final short-period orbit. However, a growing number of systems now reveal nearby planetary companions. In this talk, I will discuss recent theoretical and observational results exploring the origin and evolution of hot Jupiters, with a particular focus on those with adjacent companion planets. I show that high-eccentricity tidal migration is generally incompatible with the survival of close-in companions except in very particular scenarios. I further demonstrate that while inner companions are dynamically robust, outer companions can be driven out of the transiting plane through secular interactions, stellar evolution, and stellar obliquity, potentially explaining their apparent absence in some systems. With this in mind, I present the discovery and characterization of the TOI-4468 system as a case study, highlighting how its unique architecture (an outer companion planet, but no inner companion) constrains its dynamical history. The full observational evidence suggests that while most isolated hot Jupiters likely formed through tidal migration, systems with nearby companions preferentially assembled in dynamically cold, disk-mediated ways, revealing multiple formation pathways for close-in giant planets.

436.summary: Alumni Lecture: Batamaka Somé, \"\"Pillars of Resilience: Rural Women’s Leadership and Farmer-Centered Research for Food System Transformation in the West African Sahel\"
436.description: International Year of the Woman Farmer Series hosted by the Center for the Study of Global Gender Equity and the College of ACES Office of International Programs welcomes Illinois Alumnus Batamaka Somé, PhD in Anthropology with a Graduate Minor in Gender Relations and International Development will give a talk titled \"Pillars of Resilience: Rural Women’s Leadership and Farmer-Centered Research for Food System Transformation in the West African Sahel\".  The December 8th talk will take place at 4:00pm in 210 Levis Faculty Center and via Zoom Conventional agricultural research has too often positioned farmers as recipients and adopters of technologies developed elsewhere, rather than as active partners in generating knowledge and shaping innovation. At the same time, persistent gender inequalities and patriarchal structures have constrained women’s voice and decision-making power in households, communities, and agricultural systems—despite the central roles rural women play in farming and across food systems. In this lecture, I draw on experiences from the West African Sahel to demonstrate the empowering potential of research grounded in farmers’ realities, priorities, and knowledge. More importantly, I showcase how rural women are leveraging farmer-centred research, alongside their own transformative leadership, to strengthen resilience and drive food system transformation. Against a backdrop of insecurity, climate variability, and geopolitical volatility, these experiences reveal rural women not simply as beneficiaries of agricultural development, but as agents of innovation, leaders of change, and essential pillars of resilient food systems in the Sahel.
436.location: 210 Levis Faculty Center and via Zoom

447.summary: Siebel Center for Design Affiliate Information Session
447.description: Curious about becoming a Siebel Center for Design (SCD) Affiliate? Join us on Zoom for an informal information session for University of Illinois faculty and staff who want to learn more about the program before they apply. The SCD Affiliate Program is an interdisciplinary network of faculty and staff who lead human-centered design (HCD) work in research, teaching, and community engagement. Affiliates work with partners across campus, at peer institutions, in local communities, and in industry. In this session, we'll cover:What Affiliates do: work alongside SCD on research, teaching, and community projects, represent SCD to campus and outside partners, and advise SCD team members and HCD project leadersBenefits of membership: priority access to SCD work and maker spaces, classrooms, and event spaces, plus extra support from the SCD team for assessment and research, academic programs, marketing and programming, equipment and operations, and media contentInterdisciplinary Collaboration Themes: Technological Innovation, Community Engagement and Societal Impact, Transformative Education and Pedagogical Innovation, Health Innovation, and Entrepreneurship and Organizational DevelopmentWays to get involved: integrating HCD into a course, hosting events, leading workshops, advising projects, and moreThe application process and what to expect from the 3-year Affiliate termBring your questions! We'd love to hear how you might bring human-centered design into your work. Questions before the session? Contact Dawn Bohn, SCD Director of Faculty and Academic Engagement, at dbrehart@illinois.edu. Learn more: https://designcenter.illinois.edu/aboutscd/scdaffiliateprogram

492.summary: Quick Start Workshop: Using the Pope Tech Accessibility Tool
492.description: Get up to speed on using the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide to make Canvas pages more accessible for everyone! In this hands-on workshop, we’ll start with an overview of the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide, how it functions, what the various errors, alerts, structural elements, and features mean, and how to fix these issues on a Canvas page. Then we’ll jump into some hands-on practice using the Canvas Accessibility Guide to evaluate the accessibility of Canvas pages and remediate basic accessibility issues. We’ll discuss the limitations of the tool and what still needs to be checked manually using basic digital accessibility principles. By the end of this workshop, you’ll understand how to fix Canvas pages using the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide tool and be well on the way to creating inclusive Canvas pages that meet State and Federal accessibility standards.

576.summary: School Performance: Step Afrika! presents The Fruits of Our Labor (KCYS)
576.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. Celebrate the body as an instrument with Step Afrika!, the GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS™ title holder for the Largest Stepping Dance and the world’s leading authority on the art form of stepping. The company’s newest work, The Fruits of Our Labor, blends the power of body percussion and contemporary dance with the vibrant energy of isipantsula (a rhythmic dance originating in South African townships) and the South African gumboot dance. Long-time Step Afrika! collaborator Jakari Sherman and South African choreographer Vusi Mdoyi lead an ensemble of virtuosic dancers whose bodies become instruments—clapping, striking, and stepping in mesmerizing unison, merging rhythm and ritual, history and storytelling. Recommended for grades 3 and up Learn more about School Performance: Step Afrika! presents The Fruits of Our Labor (KCYS)

580.summary: The Neo-Futurists present The Infinite Wrench
580.description: The Chicago-based Neo-Futurists have been writing and performing 30 plays in 60 minutes since 1988. Each play offers something different: be it funny, profound, elegant, disgusting, topical, irreverent, terrifying, or a song, all are original and truthful, tackling the here-and-now, and inspired by the lived experiences of the performers. “The ingenuity and engagement of the work not only remains but has deepened . . . the ensemble maps thorny social, psychological, and political terrain with foolishness and ferocity,” says the Chicago Reader. With new plays every week, The Infinite Wrench is The Neo-Futurists’ ongoing and ever-changing attempt to shift the conventions of live performance and speak to those unreached or unmoved by traditional theatre. Learn more about The Neo-Futurists present The Infinite Wrench

596.summary: Elizabeth Rodini | A Walk through the Layered Lives of Rome
596.description: Elizabeth Rodini discusses her new book, On the Street of the Hidden Shops (Chicago, 2026), which takes a concentrated, stratigraphic approach to exploring the ancient capital. Layering finely observed details and surprising anecdotes among grander historical narratives, Rodini captures the fullness of urban life and probes the boundaries between fact and fiction. 612.summary: Mark Morris Dance Group and Music Ensemble: Music at Play
612.description: With wit, exuberance, and an irresistible sense of play, the Mark Morris Dance Group brings together four works that showcase the humor, invention, and musical imagination of Mark Morris. Designed to delight audiences of all ages, this lively program combines brilliant dancing, vivid musicality, and theatrical surprise. In My Party, Morris transforms the familiar awkwardness and excitement of a youthful gathering into a tender and funny celebration of dancing together. The wonderfully offbeat Tamil Film Songs in Stereo Pas de Deux is pure cosmic invention propelled by the rhythms of South Indian popular music. Peccadillos, set to Erik Satie's miniature piano pieces originally written for children, finds humor and humanity in a whimsical solo filled with gesture, character, and imagination. And in Sport, Morris takes inspiration from Satie's playful Sports et divertissements, turning golf, swimming, tennis, and other athletic pursuits into a witty choreographic playground. Together, these four works offer an ideal evening of the Mark Morris Dance Group: sophisticated without being solemn, playful without ever losing artistry, and animated throughout by Morris' extraordinary ability to make music visible through dance. It is a program for longtime dance lovers, first-time audiences, children, parents, grandparents—and anyone who enjoys the pleasure of watching remarkable dancers have some serious fun. Learn more about Mark Morris Dance Group and Music Ensemble: Music at Play

621.description: Landscapes in Sound and Ink explores the rich dialogue between Taiwanese visual art and music. Presented in conjunction with the Ink Shower exhibition at the Krannert Art Museum and produced in collaboration with the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies, this program brings together works inspired by landscape, memory, nature, and cultural identity.  Featuring music by Taiwanese composers for piano trio and solo piano, the concert reflects the poetic atmosphere of ink painting traditions through sound, evoking mountains, water, mist, and shifting emotional landscapes. Through the interplay of visual art and music, audiences are invited to experience how musical textures and colors parallel the expressive brushwork and spatial imagination found in Taiwanese ink paintings. This collaborative event celebrates Taiwan’s artistic heritage while fostering cross-cultural understanding through music and visual art. This event is free to attend. Musicians Chi-Chen Wu, piano; Sam Ou, cello, Yu-Kun Hsiang, violin-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------Free speech and academic freedom are foundational to our university’s missions of discovery and exploration. 632.summary: Seth Stewart: From Passion to Purpose
632.description: Join performer and educator, Seth Stewart, as he shares valuable and relatable lessons he’s learned in his journey to a successful career as an actor, dancer, choreographer, and leading performing arts educator. Audience questions will be welcomed during a Q&A session following Stewart’s talk. Stewart was an original cast member of Hamilton and performed in other Broadway shows including Sweet Charity and In the Heights. He has toured the world with popular artists such as Madonna, Jennifer Lopez, Mariah Carey, and more; appeared in movies like Sex and the City: The Movie and Music and Lyrics; as well as choreographed for the television show Bull, the Nickelodeon Kids’ Choice Awards, among others. In 2025, Stewart published his first book, Follow Your Vision, Live Your Truth, a memoir chronicling his journey from Broadway to a decade-long transformational spiritual journey that led him back to nature and his heart. Today, he serves as a performance coach and guest speaker through his company, Performer’s Edge, which provides coaching, courses, and workshops for pre-professional and professional artists – giving them the tools to succeed in the entertainment industry. Stewart is also the founder of True Kings Academy, a mentorship program supporting men with leadership skills through spiritual embodiment, mental health wellness, and wealth mindset. This event is sponsored by the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs. Learn more about Seth Stewart: From Passion to Purpose

633.description: On Thursday, February 4th we will hear from Nini Zhou, Ph.D. Student in the College of Media at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Becoming Neoliberal Subjects: Algorithmic Governance of Feminist Activism in China\" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.   In this talk, Nini Zhou discusses how algorithmic governance shapes feminist activism and produces neoliberal subjectivity in China. While existing scholarship has examined how neoliberal logics are embedded in feminist activism in China (Liu, 2023; Peng, 2021; Yin, 2022), less attention has been paid to how neoliberal logics embedded in technological structures shape feminist activism. To address this gap, this project focuses on how algorithmic governance in China structures visibility, participation, and value of feminist activism, thereby producing self-governing subjects. Algorithmic governance here refers to platform mechanisms functioning as infrastructures of digital governance, including content recommendation, search ranking, hashtag moderation, and traffic distribution. These mechanisms not only shape what content becomes visible, whose voices are amplified, and which forms of feminist expression are permitted or suppressed, but also produce regulatory frameworks for user practices in feminist activism.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

638.summary: Louie Palu | The Idea of North in Literature and Photography
638.description: Palu’s talk centers on distinct representations of the Arctic in literature and the visual arts, exploring this often-misunderstood region as both imagined otherworld and real-life landscape. Palu is especially interested in how texts such as John Milton’s epic Paradise Lost (1667) and Mary Shelley’s novel Frankenstein (1818) imagine the Arctic in the early decades of polar exploration, creating literary topographies which impact subsequent work not only in literature but the visual arts as well, including Palu’s ﬁlm and photography. Across these various media, Palu shows how inherited notions of the Arctic shape present-day discourses on subjects including climate change, resource extraction, indigenous rights, colonialism, and the militarization of polar territory. Mike Marshall, a three-time Grammy nominee, has released more than 40 recordings and is celebrated for his fluency across bluegrass, jazz, classical, and Brazilian traditions. George Meyer brings a distinctive compositional voice shaped by both classical and fiddle traditions, with commissions and performances spanning major festivals and venues nationwide. Together, these longtime collaborators revisit and expand the repertoire of Edgar Meyer’s landmark project Short Trip Home, along with new works written for this ensemble, blending their individual and collective talents in an extraordinary program. 664.description: Thank you for your interest in the lunch series on \"Gender Equity in an Inequitable Era\".  On Thursday, February 11th we will hear from Felisa Reynolds, Associate Professor in Department of French and Italian at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Maryse Condé: Gender, and the Racial Logic of Francophone Classification \" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.  This presentation draws from Dr. Reynolds' book project French or Francophone Literature: The Legacy of the Manifesto for a World Literature (Edinburgh University Press, forthcoming), which examines why the distinction between French and Francophone literature remains stubbornly intact twenty years after the publication of the manifest Pour une littérature-monde (“For a World Literature in French”), and what that persistence reveals about the racial logic organizing literary consecration in France. The chapter on Maryse Condé, which this presentation examines in detail, focuses on the reception of her work within the French literary field and argues that her decades-long exclusion from the Nobel Prize in Literature and from the highest echelons of French literary recognition was not incidental but structural, organized by the intersection of race and gender in ways that the field has never been asked to name, let alone justify.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

685.summary: Sinfonia da Camera: From Brahms with Love
685.description: Celebrating Valentine’s weekend, this program centers on the music of Johannes Brahms, whose works embody warmth, lyricism, and profound emotional depth. Alongside his music, Clara Schumann’s Konzertsatz in F Minor offers a compelling opening, reflecting her distinctive voice as both composer and pianist, as well as her close and deeply intimate artistic friendship with Brahms. Brahms’s Hungarian Dances (Nos. 1, 3, and 10) bring vibrant energy and rhythmic vitality, drawing on folk traditions with characteristic refinement. At the heart of the program, the Double Concerto in A Minor, performed by violinist Lucia Lin and cellist Owen Young, unfolds as an intimate musical dialogue of two voices in expressive conversation. The concert concludes with Brahms’s Symphony No. 2 in D Major, a radiant and expansive work whose pastoral beauty offers a luminous and deeply affectionate close. 697.summary: Seminar Series - Professor Brenda Wilson, Dept. of Microbiology
697.description: Beyond the Point-of-No-Return - Designer Toxin-Mediated Biothreats Bio: Brenda Anne Wilson, Ph.D., is a professor of microbiology and the Associate Director of Undergraduate Education in the School of Molecular & Cellular Biology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). She holds joint appointments in pathobiology at the College of Veterinary Medicine and in biomedical and translational sciences at the Carle Illinois College of Medicine. She is the Illinois Faculty Fellow for Sandia National Laboratories in the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Innovation.   After completing her B.A. in biochemistry and German from Barnard College at Columbia University, she was a DAAD graduate fellow of biochemistry at the Ludwig-Maximilians Universität München in Germany, studying virus labeling for in vivo tracking. She then earned her M.A. and Ph.D. degrees in chemistry from the Johns Hopkins University, where she received the Ernest M. Marks Achievement Award and an AAUW doctoral fellowship to study antibiotic biosynthesis. She began her studies on bacterial pathogenesis and bacterial protein toxins as an NIH-postdoctoral fellow in microbiology at Harvard Medical School, and during her first tenured faculty appointment in biochemistry at Wright State University School of Medicine.   Wilson's current research focuses on the host-microbe interface; bacterial pathogenesis and bacterial protein toxins; development of anti-toxin and toxin-based biologics; and comparative and functional genomic technologies and applications involving microbiomes in health and disease.

715.summary: Midori, violin with Festival Strings Lucerne
715.description: It has been more than 30 years since the celebrated violinist Midori graced the stage of the Foellinger Great Hall. Midori, once a child prodigy, is now a violin superstar recognized as a visionary educator and humanitarian whose multiple nonprofit organizations bring music to children and underserved communities. The United Nations appointed Midori a Messenger of Peace in 2007; she was named a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2021. “In her hands,” said Roberto Prosseda when conferring the 2025 Cremona Musica Award, “the violin is not only an instrument—it becomes a voice for humanity itself.” Midori has enjoyed a longstanding partnership with the Festival Strings Lucerne, a brilliant European chamber ensemble under the leadership of Daniel Dodds. This concert features two works by Beethoven: Egmont, Overture and Symphony No. 2 in D major, op. 36, as well as Violin concerto in D major, op. 35 by Tchaikovsky, and works by Maurice Ravel and Helena Winkelman, both of which pay homage to Haydn. Learn more about Midori, violin with Festival Strings Lucerne

716.description: “Theatre is a doorway,” says illusionist Scott Silven. “A place where we gather in the dark, drawn together by stories that remind us who we are, who we were, and who we might become. It’s where we witness the impossible, feel the weight of the past, and step into the unknown, together. And The Lost Things is about that unknown.” A joyful exploration of wonder, memory, and shared experience, Silven’s awe-inspiring 75-minute show reveals the mysterious side of human nature through breathtaking illusions and an evocative narrative. Directed by Graham McLaren and designed by Jamie Vartan, The Lost Things reminds you that even in loss, there is beauty to be found—and that sometimes, getting lost is the first step toward truly finding yourself. Suitable for ages 12 and up. Krannert Center is a proud co-commissioner of The Lost Things Learn more about Scott Silven's The Lost Things

735.description: Thank you for your interest in the lunch series on \"Gender Equity in an Inequitable Era\".  On Thursday, February 25th we will hear from Thais Duarte Zappelini, Post Doc with the Brasillinois Initiative at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Transnational Feminisms, Democracy, and Gender Justice in Brazil: Legacies and Challenges of the 1988 Constitution\" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.  During Brazil’s 1987 Constituent Assembly debates, congresswoman Rose de Freitas declared: “Women demand compliance with the Charter of Rights that the country signed with the United Nations. Either Brazil honors this commitment or withdraws and breaks ties with the United Nations.” Her statement reflected a broader feminist strategy that linked domestic constitutional reform to international human rights commitments. Freitas was one of only 26 women elected to the National Constituent Assembly and had recently returned from the Moscow Conference, which brought together more than 2,300 Latin American women to discuss shared legal and social struggles. Rather than aligning strictly with party agendas, Brazilian women parliamentarians formed the Lipstick Lobby, a cross-party coalition that prioritized gender equality. Their activism contributed to the inclusion of gender-sensitive provisions in the 1988 Constitution and unfolded within a broader context of global feminist mobilization shaped by the United Nations Decade for Women (1975 1985) and the rise of transnational feminist mobilization in Latin America during the 1970s and 1980s.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

739.summary: Up Against Erasure | “Mitsuki: the In-Between” Film Screening and Discussion
739.description: “Mitsuki: The-In Between” is a documentary that follows Mitsuki, a woman of Japanese and Korean descent, as she embarks on a deeply personal journey to uncover the forgotten history of the Jeju April 3rd Massacre—one of Korea’s most tragic and silenced events. Caught between cultures, languages, and generations, Mitsuki navigates the emotional and historical in-between, tracing the scars of her family's past and the legacy of unresolved trauma. Her search becomes a quiet but powerful act of remembrance, bridging identity and memory, silence and truth.  After the screening, respondents Roderick Wilson (East Asian Languages and Cultures and History), Anna Jungeun Lee (East Asian Languages and Cultures), and Jinhee J. Lee (History Professor and Asian Studies Chair at Eastern Illinois University) will discuss the film in the context of the “Up Against Erasure” theme and then open up for audience questions. Film runtime: 47 minutes Directed by Ho-Geun Yang Produced by KBS Cosponsored by the Asian American Cultural Center, the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies, Department of East Asian Languages & Cultures, and the Spurlock Museum of World Cultures.

742.description: Experience the premiere of There's a Ghost in Everything, a new immersive work from Zach Morris, Co-Artistic Director of Third Rail Projects. Blending dance, theater, storytelling, and song, this inviting production unfolds all around the audience, drawing guests into a village where it is always autumn and a festival honoring the community’s ghosts is underway. Along the way, audiences help performers weave together fragments of stories in real time, creating a deeply personal and shared theatrical experience. Their work has been praised as “haunting, hallucinatory, and profoundly intimate” by Vogue and “wildly imaginative” by The New Yorker. Audience should be aware that this is an interactive show, and throughout the show, you'll be invited to help out. Audience members may choose if and how to participate in these invitations in whatever way makes sense for them. 745.summary: Routes, Encounters, Destinations in Medieval Asia (ca. 500–1500)
745.description: This conference, organized by Gian Piero Persiani (EALC) and Adam Newman (Religion), will bring together scholars working across disciplines to explore how movement, exchange, and place-making shaped the medieval Asian world. Throughout history, people, objects, and knowledge have been on the move, crossing borders, merging in unexpected ways, and continually reshaping cultural and political landscapes. Movement, however, is never abstract—it unfolds through and between places both real and imagined: between origins and destinations, in cities and across frontiers, and along seas, rivers, deserts, and pilgrimage routes. Movement and destination thus exist in a dynamic and dialogical relationship, each defining and transforming the other. This conference examines these entwined histories of mobility and emplacement in Medieval South, Central, and East Asia between 500 and 1500 CE. Participants will approach the topic from diverse methodological and theoretical perspectives, exploring how travel, exchange, and encounter produced religious missions and pilgrimages; facilitated the transmission, translation, and localization of texts and ideas; fostered multilingualism and intertextuality; and animated networks of trade and diplomacy. Equally important will be attention to the physical and imagined sites that anchored these processes—urban centers, frontier zones, ports of exchange, sacred landscapes, and celebrated sites of natural beauty.  Proposed themes include:Pilgrimage and sacred geographies: routes, shrines, and travelers.Routes and networks of knowledge: monastic and scholarly communities, texts, and maps.Cityscapes and landscapes: ports, borderlands, and scenic sites.Multilingualism and translation: linguistic crossings and literary exchange.Trade, objects, and material culture: movement of commodities and artistic forms.

769.description: KODO is an internationally renowned ensemble dedicated to exploring the limitless rhythmic possibilities of traditional Japanese taiko drumming. The name “KODO” evokes both the “heartbeat,” the primal source of rhythm, and “children of the drum,” reflecting the group’s spirit of vitality and curiosity. Since debuting in 1981, KODO has performed over 7,500 times across more than 50 countries, focusing on cultural connection and human unity. Based on Sado Island off the northwest coast of Japan, KODO blends three core elements in performance: reimagined folk traditions, works by leading composers, and original creations shaped by global influences. Their newest production, Luminance, offers a striking view of KODO’s ever-evolving artistry—fusing powerful taiko with refined theatricality, dynamic choreography, and moments of shimmering stillness. The result is an immersive concert experience that pulses with energy, precision, and a radiant sense of shared human rhythm. Learn more about KODO presents LUMINANCE

776.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. KODO ignites the stage with the power of Japanese taiko drumming, transforming rhythm into a visceral, full-body experience. Their name means both “heartbeat” and “children of the drum”—a dual spirit that pulses through every performance with intensity, precision, and joy. Since their 1981 debut, KODO has captivated audiences in over 50 countries, sharing a unifying “One Earth” vision that transcends language and culture through sound. Rooted on Japan’s Sado Island, KODO’s artistry blends reimagined folk traditions, bold contemporary compositions, and original works shaped by their global encounters over the years. 780.description: Oscar-nominated filmmaker Sam Green collaborates with National Book Critics Awardee and environmentalist Rebecca Solnit for the latest of his “live cinema” experiences. In Green’s work, documentary film meets live original music with Green’s own live narration. It’s “a singular experience, and a collective one, with the potential for human connection and human errors” notes The New York Times. Trees is a profoundly moving study of humankind’s relationship to our earthly cohabitants, the silent witnesses to all of humanity across countless events and generations, putting humanity’s place into perspective. Directed and performed by Sam Green with cinematography by Yoni Brook, and featuring actress Judi Dench, poet laureate Ada Limón, scientists, and stories from around the world, Trees marks Green’s most ambitious film yet. Trees is produced by ArKtype and Josh Penn and supported in part by the National Endowment for the Arts. Commissioning partners: The Boston Symphony Orchestra; New World Symphony; Oregon Symphony Orchestra; Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Wiener Festwochen; Barbican Centre; Holland Festival; Stanford Live @ Stanford University; Duke Arts @ Duke University, Durham, NC; The Arts Center at NYU Abu Dhabi; Green Music Center of Sonoma State University; and Arizona Arts Live at University of Arizona Learn more about Sam Green presents Trees

783.summary: Patricia Owens Book Talk \"Erased: A History of International Thought Without Men\"
783.description: Patricia Owens Book Talk: Erased: A History of International Thought Without Men. How did women help create the study of international relations, and why were they subsequently written out of its history? Drawing on her book Erased, Patricia Owens explores the ideas, lives, and work of women who shaped the field in twentieth-century Britain. Moving between universities and other centers of intellectual and political life, she examines how gender, race, and institutional power shaped both the production of knowledge and the histories later told about it. The talk considers what recovering these women’s contributions reveals about intellectual erasure and the possibilities for rethinking the history of international thought. Patricia Owens FBA FRHistS is a professor of international relations at the University of Oxford and currently a Leverhulme Major Research Fellow, 2026–29.

787.summary: 2027 Gryphon Lecture: School Book Lists and the Civic Education of U.S. Teens: from 1950 to Texas
787.description: Jonna Perrillo, education historian and professor of English education at the University of Texas at El Paso, will deliver the 2027 Gryphon Lecture hosted by the Center for Children's Books in the School of Information Sciences. She will present \"School Book Lists and the Civic Education of U.S. Teens: from 1950 to Texas.\" Bio: Jonna Perrillo's scholarship focuses on humanities education and social citizenship formation, both historically and in contemporary schools. She is the author of three books: Uncivil Rights: Teachers, Unions, and the Battle for School Equity (winner of the New Scholar Book Award from the American Education Research Association, 2013) and Educating the Enemy: Teaching Nazis and Mexicans in the Cold War Borderlands (winner of the Southwest Book Award from the Border Regional Library Association, 2023, and the Bolton-Cutter Prize from the Western History Association, 2022, and Uncensored: Educators Speak Out on Teaching in the Time of Book Bans (Harvard Education Press, 2026). Her writing and research have been featured in The New York Times, The Washington Post, TIME magazine, the Boston Review, Education Week, Slate, Post45, The 74 and on PBS and National Public Radio. With Dr. Andrew Newman, she is the three-time co-director of the National Endowment for the Humanities Summer Institute for Teachers, “Making the Good Reader and Citizen: The History of Literature Instruction in American Schools.” In June 2026, she and Newman co-published the open access report \"Atomized English: Fewer Whole Books, More Isolated Learning Experiences.\"

814.summary: Food For Thought | Shelley Weinberg & Josue David Cisneros
814.description: Food for Thought: A series of public events featuring research and creative projects by recent CAS Associates and Fellows. We are delighted to showcase the work of some of our most productive and creative faculty in this informal series of intellectually and spiritually invigorating presentations. You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty. 11:00am-11:45am: Shelley Weinberg, CAS Associate 2025-26, Philosophy  Locke's Epistemological System  Locke’s Essay concerning Human Understanding launched a century of “British Empiricism.” Professor Shelley Weinberg offers a new and comprehensive interpretation of his natural epistemology (how we have certain knowledge and justified probable beliefs about the natural world), his religious epistemology (how we have justified—or not—beliefs in revelation), and his view of intellectual and moral virtue (what we should believe and how we should act). By revealing a method of what Professor Weinberg calls “rational regulation,” she elucidates a heretofore unrecognized and unarticulated comprehensive systematicity to Locke’s epistemology, its relation to his moral theory, and the role of education in the development of intellectual (epistemic) and moral virtue. Noon-12:45pm: Josue David Cisneros, CAS Associate 2025-26, Communication More to come!

883.summary: The Poet as Seismograph: Ukrainian and Yiddish Poetry of the 1920s and Beyond  A Conference at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign
883.description: The conference \"The Poet as Seismograph: Ukrainian and Yiddish,” explores the parallels and convergences of Yiddish and Ukrainian poetry of the modernist era and beyond, tracing the interaction between poets and poetry in the two languages. In the first quarter of the twentieth century Kyiv and Kharkiv were major centers of new poetry in both languages. Ukrainian and Yiddish poets of the 1920s and 30s imagined their work as sounding boards and listening devices, sensitive to the reverberations of their era. Their poetry transmitted the political and social changes of their time, the sounds generated by new technologies and the pulse of the urban landscape. In 1924 a group of Kyiv Yiddish writers called their movement “Antenna,” for example. The same motif appears around a hundred years later.  The title work of Ukrainian poet Serhii Zhadan’s 2023 poetry collection Antenna (Antena) speaks of an antenna that both drips with blood but also captures unseen “signals of love from the atmosphere.” Specialists in both Ukrainian and Yiddish trace this theme and more in the conference and the volume to follow. The transnational, comparative, multilingual, and historical perspectives offered by this conference are particularly important in our era of heightened nativism and tunnel vision. The two literatures—Yiddish and Ukrainian—have come to the brink of extinction, and Ukrainian culture and Ukraine are currently under threat, making scholarly attention even more important.

901.summary: Brown Bag Series- Denial, Deterrence, and Disenchantment: Why Many Never Immigrate
901.description: This book complements abundant research on immigrants by contributing novel data, knowledge, and theories about those who might have immigrated but did not, despite the benefits of migration to immigrants and migrant-origin and migrant-destination societies. The book examines three mechanisms that reduce immigration: denial of visas, deterrence of many from applying for visas, and ex-immigrants' disenchantment with immigration. Jacob Thomas extends the push-pull model of migration into a push-retain-pull-repel model that better explains why potential immigrants remain ambivalently immobile, providing evidence that retain factors in origin societies and repel factors in destination societies counteract and outweigh the push and pull factors that motivate immigration. Might-have-been-immigrants' narratives reveal an (im)mobility paradox: the factors that facilitate migration—socio-economic resources and social ties—also often impede immigration across different stages of the life course. Finally, examining denial, deterrence, and disenchantment alongside each other stimulates readers to think more globally about inequalities in migratory opportunities by revealing how countless people who never immigrate due to either denial, deterrence, or disenchantment are socio-economically stratified with respect to one another in ways that mirror theories of how immigrants are stratified in destination societies.

At ISU, he is the chair of the Twelve Thousand Bombs seminar series on nuclear weapons. Outside academia, he is a writer and scientific consultant for the YouTube channels \"In a Nutshell\" by Kurzgesagt and \"PBS Space Time\" by PBS Digital Studio, with writing credits on nearly 100 videos with combined view counts of a billion. 916.description: Thank you for your interest in the lunch series on \"Gender Equity in an Inequitable Era\".  On Thursday, April 1st we will hear from Maria Alejandra Garcia, Assistant Professor in Department of Natural Resources and Environmental Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Her talk, \"Women, Environment, and Gender Backlash in the Global South\" will be in-person and also offered virtually through Zoom.  Lunch will be provided for in-person attendees.  Despite decades of investment, gender equality in agricultural and natural resource-dependent contexts in the Global South remains far from realized. While women’s access to services such as extension and finance has improved, severe inequalities persist; women continue to face limited access to land, technologies, and inputs, alongside disproportionately heavy workloads and high rates of violence. Efforts by community-based groups, policy initiatives, and development projects have focused on empowering women to bridge these gaps. However, increasing women’s participation in spaces where they have historically been marginalized can also trigger backlash. Recent studies show that programs promoting women’s decision-making and challenging traditional social expectations can generate gender backlash, manifesting as household conflict, increased workloads, and violence against women. Yet, there remains a critical lack of in-depth research explaining how and why this backlash emerges within agricultural and socio-ecological systems.  This series is co-sponsored by the LAS Office of Inclusive Excellence.

927.description: The symposium will explore the timely field convergence of posthumanism and environmental design, especially with regard to how the posthumanist perspective can challenge, guide and even inspire new ways of thinking about the environment and the life that is dependent on it. This in turn can offer new insights into landscape design and the ways that designers think about animals and plants. Part of the mission of the symposium will be to explore and critique what ensues from this perspective. Several provocative questions follow from this approach:· For whom do we design? How can humans coexist in a world shared with animals? What happens when we conceive of animals and plants as architects? What happens when we conceive of animals and plants as clients? We will engage these and many more queries about the impact of newly emerging understandings of agentic and communicative capabilities beyond the human. The symposium will bring together scholars, artists, design professionals and students to consider how we might actualize the principles of multi-species cohabitation and co-design. Public lectures, participatory events, the showcasing of student design work, and transdisciplinary collaborative discussions will take place.

951.description: The Slavic Reference Service, in collaboration with the Department of Slavic Languages and Literatures at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is pleased to announce the inaugural Balkan Research Forum. This forum aims to spotlight Balkan studies and bring together scholars in all disciplines and at all stages of the research process to discuss the theme “Shifting Borders and Identities in the Balkans.” More than simply lines on a map, borders are fluid entities that can be contested, crossed, and intensely personal – extending beyond geographic spaces to shape language, memory, nationality, and belonging. The Balkans have been profoundly impacted by changing borders and by shifting political, social, and cultural landscapes, as well as global dynamics. From the fall of empires and the redrawing of state boundaries to the emergence of new nations, migration, displacement, and the persistence of cultural communities across borders, the region provides a unique opportunity to explore the intersection of territory and identity.  The inaugural Balkan Research Forum invites proposals examining how changing borders have influenced the ways individuals and communities understand identity, including nationality, ethnicity, language, religion, and memory. We particularly invite proposals that examine broader global dynamics that influence Balkan borders and identities.  We welcome contributions from scholars at all career stages and encourage graduate students, postdoctoral researchers, librarians, and archivists to submit proposals.  Participants are welcome to present in any language, but we ask that an accompanying English translation of any remarks and/or materials be provided.  The inaugural Balkan Research Forum will be held on April 8-9, 2027. Those interested in presenting should submit an abstract by February 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m., CST. Zoom details will be shared the week of the forum.  If you are interested in submitting a proposal, please do so here: 202

989.description: Layli Long Soldier is the author of the collections We (Graywolf, 2026), and Whereas (Graywolf Press, 2017), which won the National Book Critics Circle award, the 2018 PEN/Jean Stein Book Award, and was a finalist for the National Book Award. She also wrote the chapbook Chromosomory (Q Ave Press, 2010), and her work has been widely anthologized in books like Native Voices (Tupelo Press, 2019) and The Larger Voice (NACF, 2022). On Whereas, poet Dean Rader remarks, “What is especially compelling about Long Soldier is that she not only undermines language, she undermines form as well. Elsewhere, I have written about the importance of ‘compositional resistance’ for Native poets. By this, I refer to how a poet composes her poem, the form it takes, how it looks on the page, how its typography expresses itself. Whereas is a masterful example of compositional resistance.” Her poems and critical work have appeared in POETRY Magazine, The New York Times, American Poet, The American Reader, The Kenyon Review, BOMB, American Indian Journal of Culture and Research, PEN America, and The Brooklyn Rail, among many others. In 2015, Long Soldier was awarded a National Artist Fellowship from the Native Arts and Cultures Foundation and a Lannan Literary Fellowship for Poetry. She was awarded a Whiting Writer’s Award in 2016 and was shortlisted for the Griffin Poetry Prize in 2018. In 2021, she received an Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature and the Michael Murphy Memorial Poetry Prize in the UK. Long Soldier earned a BFA from the Institute of American Indian Arts and an MFA from Bard College. She teaches in the MFA Creative Writing Program at the Institute of American Indian Arts and serves as the 2024-25 Endowed Chair at Texas State University. She resides in Santa Fe, New Mexico. Event cosponsored by the Spurlock Museum of World Cultures.

996.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. Grammy-nominated children’s artist Uncle Jumbo layers heartfelt lyrics with high-energy music and interactive dance-alongs that get audiences moving together, inspiring young people to dream big, care for one another, and celebrate what makes them unique. A Texas-born son of a disco and reggae DJ, Uncle Jumbo got his start at age four, playing accordion with touring Zydeco bands on his Aunt Helen’s Louisiana porch. Known for his uplifting spirit and magnetic stage presence, he began creating music for children after the birth of his daughter. Her diagnosis with a rare liver disease, and surgery at only three weeks old, sparked a profound gratitude for life and a mission to help raise generations of positive, loving people as One Big Family. “Imagine that somewhere in the untapped treasures of the late Prince’s legendary vault of music is an album made for kids . . . That’s what Uncle Jumbo sounds like.” (Houston Press) Recommended for grades Pre K – 2 Learn more about School Performance: Uncle Jumbo (KCYS)

1004.description: Taste Makers: Craft & Credit in the Age of AIApril 17, 2027 | Siebel Center for Design, University of Illinois Urbana-ChampaignWhen anyone can generate a screen, a persona, or a prototype in seconds, making things is no longer the hard part. Knowing what’s good is. As AI takes on more of the effort in design work, a designer's value shifts to taste — the craft, care, and point of view to decide what to build, who it's for, and what's worth putting your name on.Last year, UX Days explored how designers work within systems in flux. This year, we turn to the people shaping what comes out of those systems. Together, we'll ask: What makes great work great, how do we develop the taste to recognize it, and who gets the credit when people and machines make things together?Through keynotes, workshops, and conversations, UX Day 2027 bridges the critical and the practical, inviting students, educators, and professionals to sharpen the taste, craft, and ownership that make design human — no matter what tools help us get there. Currently accepting proposals for breakout sessions and keynote speakers. Find more information here.

1009.description: Sinfonia da Camera concludes its season with a program that explores transformation and renewal through music of extraordinary scope and intensity. David DeBoor Canfield’s Overture: Threnody for the Victims of Military Aggression opens the concert with a work of solemn reflection and contemporary resonance. Stravinsky’s Firebird follows, illuminating the orchestra with its vivid orchestration and mythic narrative of rebirth. Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat Major, conducted from the piano by Ian Hobson, showcases a bold integration of virtuosity and symphonic structure. The season concludes with Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 5, a powerful journey from darkness to affirmation. With its sweeping themes and triumphant conclusion, the symphony offers a fitting culmination to a season defined by expressive depth and artistic ambition. Program: David DeBoor Canfield: Overture: Threnody for the Victims of Military Aggression Igor Stravinsky: The Firebird Franz Liszt: Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat Major, S.124 Ian Hobson, piano and conductor Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky: Symphony No. 5 in E Minor, Op. 64 Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: Firebird Finale

1014.description: The Jupiter String Quartet chose its name because the planet Jupiter was prominent in the night sky at the time of the quartet’s formation in 2001. A particularly intimate group consisting of violinists Mélanie Clapiès and Meg Freivogel, violist Liz Freivogel (Meg’s older sister), and cellist Daniel McDonough (Meg’s husband, Liz’s brother-in-law), the ensemble's star continues to shine brightly as an important voice in the world of chamber music, exuding an energy that is at once friendly, knowledgeable, and adventurous. This program presents Mozart’s String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, “Dissonance” and Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 12 in E-flat Major, Op. 127, alongside Azerbaijani composer Franghiz Ali-Zadeh’s Oasis (String Quartet No. 4). The evocative 1998 composition captivates with its mixture of sounds and textures, moods and pictures. Program: Mozart: String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, K.465, “Dissonance” Franghiz Ali-Zadeh: “Oasis” (String Quartet No. 4) Beethoven: String Quartet No. 12 in E-flat Major, Op. 127 Learn more about Jupiter String Quartet

1016.summary: School Performance: Honolulu Theatre for Youth | Joseph Kekuku and the Voice of the Steel Guitar (KCYS)
1016.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. It’s the late 1800s, a time of invention. Trains, steamboats, cameras, even electricity are new at the King’s palace in Honolulu. Eleven-year-old Joseph Kekuku accidentally strikes the strings of his guitar with a bolt from a railroad track and unlocks a brand new sound. Hawaiian music—and the music of America—is never the same. Playwright Moses Goods, one of Hawaiʻi’s most prominent theatre artists, in collaboration with Kealakai Center for Pacific Strings, captures the true story of Joseph Kekuku’s invention of the steel guitar (kīkā kila). The multimedia production features a live Hawaiian slide guitar soundtrack and projections as it celebrates innovation, engineering, and the global exchange of ideas and sound. Rich in history, the play also looks forward and encourages children of today to celebrate their voice, culture, and sense of curiosity. Recommended for grades 2-8 Learn more about School Performance: Honolulu Theatre for Youth | Joseph Kekuku and the Voice of the Steel Guitar (KCYS)

1062.summary: sweat variant presents adaku, part 2: she shivers with it.
1062.description: Created by sweat variant, the acclaimed partnership between artist and MacArthur Fellow Okwui Okpokwasili and director and designer Peter Born, adaku, part 2: she shivers with it. continues a speculative trilogy exploring one family’s entanglement with the transatlantic slave trade. Set in a near-future United States, part 2 investigates the embodied consequences of this violent rupture and the erasure of ancestral knowledge. When transmissions lead to sudden remembering, what is unleashed in the imagination of a young woman who's been led to believe she has no history worth remembering? What are the multitude of futures she can now imagine? sweat variant’s multidisciplinary approach invites audiences into cycles of ritual and repair. The presentation of adaku, part 2: she shivers with it. by Sweat Variant was made possible by the New England Foundation for the Arts' National Dance Project, with lead funding from the Doris Duke Foundation and the Mellon Foundation. Learn more about sweat variant presents adaku, part 2: she shivers with it.

1080.description: Experience an unforgettable evening with Audra McDonald. Widely regarded as one of the greatest performers of her generation, McDonald is the only artist to win six Tony Awards across all four acting categories, along with two Grammy Awards, an Emmy, and the National Medal of Arts. In this intimate concert setting, she brings her luminous voice and profound interpretive skill to a richly varied program of Broadway favorites, selections from the Great American Songbook, and more. Backed by her ensemble, McDonald creates a deeply personal connection with audiences, blending technical brilliance with emotional depth and storytelling mastery. Whether on stage or screen, her artistry consistently sets the standard for excellence. This special appearance promises an evening of elegance, warmth, and musical brilliance from a truly iconic performer. Learn more about An Evening with Audra McDonald

The series is designed to expand access to companion animal science knowledge, foster interdisciplinary collaboration, and support engagement across academia, industry, and the broader community. Recordings, when available, and upcoming webinar details are shared throughout the year.

1220.summary: Campus visit from the Consul General of Moldova
1220.description: Consul General Anton Lungu is the first Consul General of the Republic of Moldova to Chicago, following the Consulate's inauguration in 2025. During his visit, he hopes to build connections with the Russian, East European, and Eurasian Center and the European Union Center, raising academic awareness of Moldova and exploring opportunities for continued engagement with Illinois. 1229.description: The campus seeks to nominate sophomores and juniors for the prestigious Udall Scholarship. The Udall awards $7,000 to sophomores or juniors who are taking action to address environmental concerns and are committed to a career related to the environment. Students must be US citizens, US nationals, or US permanent residents. A successful applicant will have a GPA of 3.0 or higher and demonstrate leadership and a commitment to service. The University of Illinois may nominate up to six students for the Udall Scholarship. The campus deadline is January 25, 2027 to be considered. If you are interested in applying, please plan to attend our Udall sessions.  On Thursday December 3, 2026 from 3:30pm - 4:30pm there will be an information session and discussion with a former Udall Scholar and on Friday December 4, 2026 from 3:00pm - 4:00pm is a workshop on how to craft a Udall Application.  These sessions are being held in 514 IUB.Please note that there are also Udall awards for Native American students interested in tribal policy or health care (no need to be related to the environment).* For more information, contact the scholarships office at topscholars@illinois.edu or visit our website at Udall – National & International Scholarships Program
1229.location: Illini Union Bookstore Building, fifth floor #514, 807 S Wright St Champaign IL, 61820

1243.summary: Innovative Teaching to Excel and Advance MedEd (iTEAM)
1243.description: iTEAM is an innovative partnership with the ACGME and is guided by the ACGME Medical Educator Competencies. This academic year program explores essential components for effective teaching in medical education. Nationally recognized presenters, education specialist faculty, and instructional coaches facilitate the experience through a collaborative small-group cohort model. The program blends monthly half-day workshops with asynchronous learning and individualized coaching support. Participants receive observation, feedback, and mentoring to strengthen teaching effectiveness across clinical and educational settings. The series is approved for ACCME continuing education credit. Registration opens each Spring/Summer for the following academic year.

1306.description: ACGME – CIMED (C.O.M.P.A.S.S. PROGRAM) Assessment is essential to all levels of education, and UME and GME are no exception. With the introduction of competency and outcome-based education, and with the ACGME’s current accreditation model that includes the Milestones, the urgency for high-quality Medical Education programs to meet the needs of learners and the public has grown substantially. The program goal for C.O.M.P.A.S.S. is to enhance the assessment competencies of undergraduate and graduate medical education faculty by providing a comprehensive, experiential learning experience that equips participants with advanced skills in competency-based medical education, assessment methodology, and learner evaluation strategies. The key topics highlight:  – Competency-Based Medical Education principles – Outcome-focused assessment methods – Milestones and EPAs implementation – Practical application of assessment tools – Assessment systems development – Skills enhancement for UME and GME faculty – Strategies for effective learner evaluation Our target audience includes all UME and GME faculty, including residency and fellowship program directors, associate program directors, chairs, members of Clinical Competency Committees (CCCs), and any faculty members with major responsibility for the assessment of learners. Registration opens February 2027.

1309.description: Tech Pulse 2030 is more than just an event. It’s a movement dedicated to showcasing the brightest minds and fostering deep engagement among leaders, entrepreneurs, and changemakers. Together, we’ll explore the real-world impact of emerging technologies and chart a course for a future where responsible innovation drives progress for both businesses and society. What began in Chicago has now expanded across multiple U.S. cities and international hubs, delivering 50+ high-impact events, engaging over 50,000 professionals and academic partners, featuring 300+ world-class speakers, and advancing responsible AI conversations across 10+ industries. Tech Pulse 2030 is your platform to learn, connect, and lead—driving real progress for businesses, society, and the world we are building together. Reserve your spot today! We look forward to welcoming you to Tech Pulse 2030 and sharing this exciting journey with you. Hosted by AI 2030 http://www.ai2030.org AI 2030 is a global initiative committed to mainstreaming Responsible AI by 2030. Through cross-sector collaboration, capacity building, and inclusive programming, AI 2030 empowers leaders, organizations, and communities to harness AI for the benefit of humanity. Chicago AI Council https://www.chicagoaicouncil.org The Chicago AI Council is committed to a future where AI benefits everyone—from Chicago to the world. Its mission is driven by three core priorities: (1) making Chicago the global capital of responsible AI by convening international leaders through forums, awards, and innovation showcases; (2) fueling AI innovation by uniting research, entrepreneurship, and industry to build and scale trustworthy, real-world solutions; and (3) turning AI education into real job opportunities by preparing students and workers for emerging, high-growth roles across the AI economy. 1310.summary: Implementers and Innovators: Industry Perspectives on the Energy-Water-Compute Nexus
1310.description: Energy-Water-Compute Nexus Seminar SeriesImplementers and Innovators: Industry Perspectives on the Energy-Water-Compute NexusWednesday, December 2, 2026 12:00–1:30 p.m. Discovery Partners Institute (DPI) 200 S. Wacker Drive, 20th Floor, Chicago, IL CR 2032 Hybrid — In person + virtual *Lunch will be provided at 11:30 AM for in-person attendees. In-person registration is limited. Session Description |  Discovery Partners Institute, 200 S. Wacker Drive, Chicago, 20th floor · Hybrid (in person and virtual) The Energy-Water-Compute Nexus series is building a community around one of the defining infrastructure questions of our time: how to power, cool and site AI computing responsibly. In Session 1, Data Centers as Systems - An Introduction, we covered the fundamentals of how compute, energy and water connect inside a modern data center. Session 2 Unasked questions: Research challenges in data centers that break the silos brought academics, independent consultants, and investors together on the research questions no one is asking yet. Session 3 hands the floor to the people building and deploying these systems. Industry engineers, startups, and technology leaders will go beyond Data Center 101 to the challenges that are often underestimated. Does a large data center really use less water than an office building of the same size? Even if it does, where do several gigawatts of waste heat go: into Lake Michigan, into cooling towers, or into the air? What do 1 MW racks mean for building design, when their foundation loads quickly rule out multi-story facilities? Bring your questions for an open discussion with the panel.Featured Speakers Abhishek PurohitCo-founder of SPARK, hosted by mHUB Said Al-HallajCEO and Founder of NETenergy, hosted by mHUB Bill SchaumannSenior Associate Electrical Engineer, Mission Critical, Burns & McDonnell Hubertus FrankeDistinguished Research Scientist, IBM T.J. 1311.description: Faculty Entrepreneurial Leadership Program (FELP) at the University of Illinois empowers top faculty innovators to enhance the commercial and social impact of their research by transforming ideas into marketable innovations and real-world ventures. Through a series of immersive workshops led by distinguished faculty and industry experts, FELP provides foundational business knowledge, essential skills, and a collaborative community of entrepreneurial-minded faculty. 1313.description: The National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA) is hosting its monthly Colloquium Series and invites everyone to participate in the December session. Talk Title: Integrating Biophysical Interactions into AI-Guided Drug DiscoveryAbstract: While deep learning has revolutionized structural biology, traditional artificial intelligence (AI) models frequently struggle to predict dynamic behaviors, out-of-distribution specificity, and complex biophysical contexts. Bridging the gap between static pattern recognition and physical reality requires embedding fundamental biophysical constraints directly into machine-learning frameworks. We will explore recent breakthroughs that move beyond single structures into continuous conformational landscapes. Highlighting architectures like ESMDynamic, we demonstrate how sequence-based models can map residue contact dynamics and multitemperature kinetics, bypassing weeks of computationally expensive molecular dynamics simulations to automatically guide sampling pipelines. Furthermore, we will examine cross-modal composition frameworks from my group that allow domain-specific biological large language models to fuse disparate modalities—such as proteins, ligands, and peptides—by learning structural interactions directly within their internal layers. Finally, we translate these concepts into targeted engineering workflows. We will showcase how integrating geometric constraints allows tools like EZSpecificity to accurately map enzyme-substrate recognition, and how LassoESM leverages domain-adaptive pretraining to untangle the rigid lariat fold of macrocyclic peptides for de novo drug design. Together, these advancements demonstrate that embedding biophysics into AI accelerates machine learning, paving the way for experimentally viable therapeutics. Bio: Diwakar Shukla is the J. W.
