1317.description: Community Detection at Scale (CDS2027) is a workshop on research related to community structure in large networks. This will take place at the Discovery Partners Institute (DPI) in Chicago IL from May 17 to 18, 2026, and is funded by the NSF grant Collaborative Research: OAC Core: Cyber-Infrastructure for Community Detection, Extraction, and Search in Large Networks, CISE/OAC 2402559. We will have contributed and invited talks, a poster session, and software demos of new methods developed by the project. Researchers may request to give a contributed talk or poster through Microsoft CMT on one or more of the following topics: algorithms and software for community detection and community search, high performance computing for these problems, synthetic network generators, and agent-based models for community growth. The grant includes some funding for participant support to (partially) reimburse travel expenses. The deadline for submitting a talk or poster request (through Microsoft CMT) is January 15, 2027, and decisions will be announced by Feb 1, 2027. A proceedings (with short abstracts of at most two pages) will be posted to Zenodo for all talks and posters presented at the conference. Please see this document for more information.

1331.summary: Art History Visiting Lecture: Angela Miller
1331.description: Art History Visiting Lecture Angela Miller Artists and Writers on Fire Island in the Era of Global War Thursday, December 3, 5:30pm | Levis Faculty Center 210“Queer is an attitude of mind and of life.”        -Tilda Swinton This talk will explore the shared lives and works of a circle of queer artists and writers in the years around World War II. Based in New York City and Fire Island, Paul Cadmus, Jared and Margaret French, George Platt Lynes, George Tooker, Bernard Perlin, and their transatlantic literary friends gathered around Lincoln Kirstein—best known for his collaboration with George Balanchine in creating the New York City Ballet. Predating by several decades the political movement for gay rights, they collectively realized a queer world of intimate friendships and family partnerships that took shape in their enigmatic figuration, both in painting and in photography. Starkly silhouetted in dramatic scenarios on the dunes of Fire Island or in states of quiet suspension, these figurative scenarios endowed a fraught present with the power of ritual. Taking shape in the late 1930s, a form of magic or symbolic realism emerged alongside New York school abstraction, whose “triumph” overshadowed figurative art in the U.S. over the next decades. Yet in renouncing the expressive drive of modernism— for all its marketability—they engendered a new understanding of selves in continual flux, ever responsive to both the environment of nature and the vagrant desires of other selves.Angela Miller’s career as a scholar of the arts and visual culture spans from the 16th century to the late 20th, tracing the histories of colonization and nation-building, global fascism and war. Author of the prize-winning Empire of the Eye in 1993, she also led a team of scholars to bring the exceptionalist premise of so much scholarship in the field into line with the global turn in the field more generally. American Encounters (2008) engages the impact of multicultural encounters in shaping

1674.summary: Theory Seminar Series: Timothy Chan, \"3SUM Made Simpler.\"
1674.description: Abstract: Last month, a truly subquadratic algorithm for the 3SUM problem was found by Anthropic, as presented by Alman and Vassilevska Williams. Their algorithm relied on a new subroutine for rectangular matrix multiplication with selected output entries. In this talk, I will describe a different truly subquadratic randomized algorithm for 3SUM for integer inputs, found with the help of AI. It bypasses matrix multiplication techniques but instead modifies known dynamic programming algorithms for subset convolution and the zeta transform, which rely only on simple subtraction tricks via inclusion–exclusion, and so is conceptually easier to understand. The approach also leads to a refutation of the (integer) k-SUM Hypothesis for all odd k.  This is joint work with Reina Itakura, Zhiyuan Ma, and Yuancheng Yu.

1678.summary: Colloquium: Mark Neubauer, \"Convergent Intelligence for Scientific Discovery and Next-Generation AI.\"
1678.description: Refreshments Provided. Abstract:  Artificial intelligence is transforming scientific discovery, while the demands of science are creating new challenges for how intelligent systems learn, compute, and interact with the physical world. Experiments that must interpret streams of data in real time make these challenges especially concrete: predictive accuracy must be considered alongside latency, energy consumption, uncertainty, and the constraints of sensing and computation. In this talk, I will describe a research direction I call convergent intelligence: the coordinated development of learning algorithms, hardware, software, and scientific instruments, with AI itself becoming an active tool in their design. Drawing on examples from particle physics, including machine learning for particle reconstruction and intelligent pixel sensors, I will discuss how scientific requirements motivate advances in efficient inference and the integration of learning with sensing. These examples connect questions of representation and inference to the physical systems that acquire and process experimental data. I will then explore how this approach could extend to emerging computing paradigms. The central opportunity is reciprocal: AI can help design new platforms for intelligence, while those platforms can enable scientific discovery and experiments that probe the principles of learning itself. I will close with open research questions at the intersection of machine learning, computer architecture, and the physical sciences. Bio: Mark Neubauer is a Professor of Physics at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign specializing in high-energy physics, data science, and advanced computing. A Principal Investigator on the ATLAS Experiment at CERN, his research focuses on fundamental physics and real-time artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-hardware co-design for extreme-scale scientific data. 1683.summary: BIOE Seminar Series: Associate Professor Hao Wang, PhD
1683.description: Bayesian Deep Learning: From Reliable Neural Networks to Interpretable Foundation Models Abstract: While perception tasks such as visual object recognition and text understanding play an important role in human intelligence, the subsequent tasks that involve inference, reasoning, and planning require an even higher level of intelligence. The past decade has seen major advances in many perception tasks using deep learning models. In terms of higher-level inference, however, probabilistic graphical models, with their ability to expressively describe properties of variables and various probabilistic relations among variables, are still more powerful and flexible. To achieve integrated intelligence that involves both perception and inference, we have been exploring along a research direction, which we call Bayesian deep learning, to tightly integrate deep learning and Bayesian models within a principled probabilistic framework. In this talk, I will present the proposed unified framework and some of our recent work on Bayesian deep learning with various applications including interpretable large language models, network analysis, and healthcare. Biography: Hao Wang is currently an Associate Professor in the School of Information Sciences at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. Previously he was an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science at Rutgers University and a Postdoctoral Associate at the Computer Science & Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL) of MIT, working with Dina Katabi and Tommi Jaakkola. He received his PhD degree from the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, as the sole recipient of the School of Engineering PhD Research Excellence Award in 2017. He has been a visiting researcher in the Machine Learning Department of Carnegie Mellon University. 1691.summary: Using AI as a Tool, Not a Shortcut: AI Integration in RST 460's Event Planning Process
1691.description: In RST 460 (Event Management in Recreation, Sport & Tourism), students work with community partners to plan and facilitate events in the community. This fall, students in the Event Management course are using AI tools intentionally throughout their semester-long event planning process. For each component of students’ event plan, they are drafting that section with their group without the use of any technology, use an AI tool for feedback on their draft, critique the AI output for accuracy, bias, and fit with their specific attendees and event, and then revise the section (making specific note of how AI was used in that portion). The goal is not to have AI plan the events, but for students to develop their AI literacy alongside the human-centered creativity and judgment that event professionals need. My aim is to help the students become confident, but not dependent, users of AI in the event planning process. I will share how the assignments in the course are structured and the reasoning behind the design, and will also share some preliminary data about students’ experience with the AI integration into the event planning process: what they are finding useful, confusing, or surprising.

1695.summary: 2026 Game Studies and Design Showcase Keynote “Reassembling IP Norms: From Gatekeepers of Indie Games to Gamergate”
1695.description: In the first half of the 2010s, moral entrepreneurs within the medium of the video game sought cultural legitimacy. The indie games subculture provided a vanguard for this effort. Journalists, critics, academics, and other developers protected the work of successful developers through the shaming of cloners and the lionization of auteurs. Those same social mechanisms were turned outward from that subculture toward broader debates about what it meant to be a \"gamer.\" This effort to contest cultural norms in popular culture ultimately mobilized a counter-network that fueled #Gamergate, a purported reform effort about \"ethics in games journalism\" that began as a misogynistic harassment campaign against female developers and critics. Just as the networks that regulated creativity norms in indie gaming expanded their sights to wider social conflicts, the counter-network assembled around #Gamergate expanded its goals to encompass the 2016 election and beyond. Tommy Rousse is an Assistant Professor of Law and Richard W. & Marie L. Corman Scholar at the University of Illinois College of Law, where he teaches and writes about intellectual property, contracts, and the law of creative industries, focusing on video games and new media. He studies how creators, re-users, and audiences understand the rules governing creative work, and how creative communities regulate themselves where intellectual property law does not reach. Please join us for this special event. Food will be served. We hope to see you there.

1704.summary: NPRE 596 Graduate Seminar Series - Jason Hayward
1704.description: Detection, localization, and characterization of SNM in response to nuclear incidents  Abstract: Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation’s Enabling Capabilities in Technology (TECH) consortium includes three main technical areas and two-crosscutting technical areas. My group’s work fits best into the cross-cutting technical area called detection, characterization, and response methodologies and tools, and more specifically within our task related to detection, localization and characterization of special nuclear material in response to nuclear incidents. In this talk, I’ll introduce some recent and ongoing research from my group and collaborators working on this particular task. Technology developments that could improve our capability to detect, locate, characterize, assess and manage consequences related to nuclear and energetic materials are crucial to our effective response to nuclear incidents. This includes portable and wearable radiation detection systems along with advanced algorithmic approaches. It also includes the use of backscatter for single-side imaging with MeV x-rays and DT neutrons.  Bio: Jason Hayward, UCOR Fellow, is a Professor of Nuclear Engineering at the University of Tennessee and the Director of DOE/NNSA Defense Nuclear Nonproliferation's Enabling Capabilities in Technology Consortium. Hayward has over 70 peer-reviewed publications and 26 PhD graduates. He teaches classes in engineering design, radiation detection and imaging, and nondestructive assay of nuclear materials. Hayward is an ANS Fellow, an IEEE Senior Member, and INMM Senior Member. He is an Associate Editor for IEEE Transactions on Nuclear Science. He holds a PhD in Nuclear Engineering and Radiological Sciences from the University of Michigan.  Prior to his time in academia, Hayward served as a U.S. Naval Officer for eight years.

1707.summary: The Anthony J Leggett Institute for Condensed Matter Theory Seminar, André Mudry (ETH Zurich, Switzerland), \"Invertible parafermionic topological phases in one dimension\"
1707.description: Title: \"Invertible parafermionic topological phases in one dimension.\" Abstract: Invertible topological phases (ITPs) of matter have non-degenerate ground states on closed spatial manifolds. Their classification for bosonic and fermionic systems is well understood, particularly in low dimensions. Moreover, two ITPs can be combined to produce a third one in an operation that is called stacking. This produces an Abelian group structure on the bosonic and fermionic ITPs. What new structures emerge when the microscopic degrees of freedom are neither bosonic nor fermionic? In this talk, I will explore one-dimensional invertible topological phases built from parafermions, which generalize fermions to allow fractional statistics. I will introduce three cohomological invariants that classify these phases and describe their composition under stacking. Remarkably, the resulting stacking group can be non-Abelian, in contrast to its bosonic and fermionic counterparts. I will illustrate this phenomenon through explicit Hamiltonians of order-3 parafermions with ℤ₃ × ℤ₃ × ℤ₃ symmetry. These phases generate the non-Abelian group Heis(ℤ₃) ⋊ ℤ₂, where Heis(ℤ₃) is the Heisenberg group of order 27.

1719.summary: Mind in Vitro Seminar: Haohan Wang
1719.description: Abstract: Diseases are classified by clinical presentation, yet many share molecular mechanisms that no single study can reveal. Nitisinone, an herbicide that became a treatment first for tyrosinemia and later for alkaptonuria because the two diseases share a pathway, shows what such connections can offer. Finding them systematically requires analyzing hundreds of heterogeneous datasets consistently, work that has depended on bioinformaticians handling one dataset at a time. In this talk I describe how my group builds large language model agents to take on that work, and what becomes discoverable once they do. I begin with GenoTEX, a benchmark of 1,384 expert-curated gene–trait analyses over 911 cohorts, and GenoMAS, a multi-agent system that writes, executes and reviews cohort-specific code and reaches 84% of expert accuracy. The rest of the talk turns to analyses across whole corpora. Comparing the transcriptomic signatures of 1,384 disease–condition pairs recovers clinical taxonomy, links diseases it places far apart, and shows conditions such as hypertension amplifying these links. Rondo builds regulatory networks for 663 patient subgroups and compares them more than 212,000 times. Disease identity is visible from one comparison, but shared regulators become reproducible only as comparisons accumulate. This singles out 222 disease pairs, including an enteric neural crest program shared by Parkinson’s disease and gastric cancer. Finally, an exhaustive comparison of all 231 pairs among 22 human tissues finds conserved protein co-abundance clusters even between unrelated organs. Of these clusters, 379 replicate in independent proteomes, and one links three white matter disease genes through liver and bone marrow. Across these studies, agents make analysis cheap enough to repeat, and repetition turns a single observation into a quantity that can be tested. 1738.summary: From Structural Dynamics to Operations: Human–Machine Integration for Civil Infrastructure | Fernando Moreu | CEE 595 S - Structural Engineering Seminar Series
1738.description: From Structural Dynamics to Operations: Human–Machine Integration for Civil Infrastructure  Abstract: New human–machine interfaces, sensing technologies, and automated systems are expanding the capabilities of structural engineers. Advances in structural dynamics, computational modeling, embedded sensing, and control now enable engineers to interact with robotic systems in near real time, creating new opportunities for infrastructure inspection, structural assessment, construction, and experimental testing. This seminar presents research integrating structural dynamics and engineering operations through the design, simulation, and experimental validation of human–robot interfaces. Applications include Augmented Reality (AR) systems for infrastructure inspection and automated defect detection, where image-based measurements are translated directly into engineering quantities and presented intuitively to the inspector. New tracking and sensing approaches are also introduced for low-latency identification of nonlinear structural and mechanical systems. Building on these capabilities, human–robot interfaces are developed to allow structural engineers to interact directly with robotic systems and modify their operation based on engineering judgment and observed structural response. Immersive AR environments provide intuitive access to robot motion, sensing information, and controller parameters, enabling bidirectional communication between engineers and machines without removing the engineer from the decisionmaking process. Applications spanning structural inspection, construction, and manufacturing demonstrate how these technologies can connect algorithms with engineering operations. More broadly, this work illustrates a pathway toward human–machine integration in which sensing, dynamics, automation, and engineering judgment work together to address emerging challenges in civil infrastructure.    Bio: Fernando Moreu, PE, F. ASCE, is the Robert J. Stamm Professor of Adva

1742.summary: The Physics Colloquium: Brian Fields (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign) \"Big-Bang Nucleosynthesis:  the Rise of the Elements in the Early Universe\"
1742.description: Abstract: We will give an overview of the status of big-bang nucleosynthesis (BBN), which describes the production of the lightest nuclei--deuterium, 3He, 4He, and 7Li--during the first three minutes of cosmic time.   This is one of the few arenas in nature where all four fundamental forces play essential roles.  Standard BBN assumes that the simplest and most robust physics is at play, combining the Standard Model of particle physics, nuclear cross-section measurements, and the neutron lifetime; this leaves only a single free parameter--the cosmic density of baryons, i.e., ordinary matter.  We will emphasize the transformative influence of cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiments, which pin down the cosmic baryon density to exquisite precision.  This allows BBN to make tight predictions for the primordial light element abundances, which can be compared with observations:  for deuterium the agreement is spectacular, and for helium the agreement is excellent.  This CMB/BBN concordance marks a great success of the hot big bang, and BBN and the CMB together now sharply probe cosmology, neutrino physics, and dark matter physics at times around 1 second.  But this success is tempered by lithium observations that are significantly discrepant with BBN+CMB predictions;  we will summarize possible resolutions to this \"lithium problem.\"    Turning to 4He, we will present new observations that have achieved a leap in precision.  We will discuss the implications of these observations for cosmology and physics beyond the Standard Model.   We conclude with an outlook on future CMB, astronomical, and laboratory measurements that can better probe new physics in the early Universe, and help shed light on the solution to the lithium problem.

1750.summary: Condensed Matter Seminar - \"The Emergence of Time from Quantum Dynamics: An Ising-Like Symmetry Breaking\"
1750.description: In standard quantum mechanics, the dynamics of a quantum state is described in terms of time evolution. In the recently developed dual-sector dynamical framework, I propose that a quantum state can simultaneously support two complementary directions of evolution: one along time and the other along energy. At the level of observation, the question then becomes: which one organizes what we observe? I further postulate a discrete symmetry between two possible role assignments: time evolution occupies the observable slot and energy evolution the reciprocal slot, or vice versa. This resembles an Ising system in condensed matter physics. In the presence of interactions, collective ordering and spontaneous symmetry breaking can occur, leading to either ferro-like or antiferro-like phases. Both phases can give rise to a common macroscopic time, as we experience it. At low energies, the two phases may appear indistinguishable, while at higher energies or finer resolution, they may exhibit distinct behaviors that could potentially leave observable signatures in cosmology.

1781.summary: Energetic Materials Research at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory
1781.description: Abstract  Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL) is a Federally Funded Research and Development Center (FFRDC) which operates under the U. S. Department of Energy’s National Nuclear Security Administration (DOE, NNSA). The Energetic Materials Center (EMC) at LLNL develops and maintains expertise on energetic materials (high explosives, propellants, and pyrotechnics) in support of national security. An overview of research areas in the Energetic Materials Center at LLNL will be provided as well as information about upcoming internship opportunities.  This work was performed under the auspices of the U.S. Department of Energy by Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under Contract DE-AC52-07NA27344. LLNL-ABS-2026567.  About the Speaker  Emily Weerakkody is the Outreach Programs Research Scientist for the Energetic Materials Center at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (LLNL). She received a Ph.D. in Mechanical Engineering from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and joined LLNL as a postdoc in 2021 and became a staff scientist in 2024. Her graduate study was on spectroscopic signatures in the post-detonation nuclear fireball under Professor Nick Glumac. Since her hire at LLNL, she has been working on various safety and performance experiments on high explosives with colleagues in the High Explosive Applications Facility in addition to continuing research in nuclear forensics.  Host: Professor Nick Glumac

1797.description: Title: Moving Lifelines: Fixed Sites or Mobile Fleets for Volunteer-Enabled Emergency Medical Device Delivery?  Abstract: Timely use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) is critical for survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest, yet AED deployment creates value only if devices reach patients within a clinical window. We study how a city should allocate an AED budget between fixed locations and mobile fleets to maximize timely deliveries. In the fixed-location (static) system, a responder retrieves an AED before reaching the patient; in the mobile system, on-demand fleet vehicles carry AEDs for direct delivery. We develop a stochastic spatial model capturing two-leg static retrieval and mobile fleet idleness. We first characterize both pure systems. Static performance depends jointly on AED and responder density: increasing either resource eventually yields a ceiling determined by the other. Mobile deployment avoids this retrieval-geometry bottleneck, but fleet idleness and driver responsiveness discount each AED-equipped vehicle’s value. Across otherwise comparable cities, a larger population increases responder density but reduces mobile fleet idleness, producing a unique switch in the preferred pure system from mobile to static. Under identifiable conditions, small budgets can make static deployment inferior even with arbitrarily dense responders. We then solve the joint allocation problem. A log-miss reformulation reveals a scale effect of static deployment, whereas each mobile AED contributes a constant log-miss reduction. Optimal policies therefore concentrate AEDs in one channel until a channel-specific limit makes hybrid deployment relevant. Computable thresholds characterize these regimes. Using real-world data, we find that, at observed AED stocks, the calibrated model favors pure static deployment in New York City and pure mobile deployment in Singapore.  Short Bio: Jingwei Zhang is an Assistant Professor of Operations, Technology, and Informat

1804.summary: AE 590 Seminar Speaker: Ivan Bermejo-Moreno - Large-eddy simulation of transonic buffet with wind-tunnel confinement effects
1804.description: Abstract: Transonic airfoil buffet of a supercritical OAT15A airfoil at Mach 0.72 and an angle of attack of 5º is studied with high-fidelity numerical simulations that aim to replicate wind-tunnel experiments conducted at the Trisonic Wind Tunnel of the Institute of Aerodynamics, RWTH Aachen University. Large-eddy simulations with and without an equilibrium wall model, as well as different spanwise domain length and boundary treatments are performed to assess the effects of wind-tunnel confinement (from the top/bottom and side walls) on the observed buffet-cycle dynamics, including oscillatory lambda-shock motion, shock-induced separation, and wake vortex shedding. Comparisons with Schlieren and particle-image velocimetry (PIV) experimental measurements will be presented, including modal analyses employing spectral proper orthogonal decomposition (SPOD) techniques. Bio: Ivan Bermejo-Moreno is an associate professor in the Aerospace and Mechanical Engineering Department of the Viterbi School of Engineering at the University of Southern California. He received an Aeronautical Engineer degree from the Polytechnic University of Madrid, Spain, followed by M.Sc. and Ph.D. degrees in aeronautics from the California Institute of Technology. Afterwards, he held a postdoctoral research fellowship at the Center for Turbulence Research, Stanford University/NASA Ames Research Center. His research combines numerical methods, physical modeling, and high-performance computing for the simulation and analysis of turbulent fluid flows involving multi-physics phenomena. Prof. Bermejo-Moreno is an Associate Fellow of the American Institute of Aeronautics and Astronautics, and the recipient of the NSF CAREER Award, the NASA Early Career Faculty Award, the Fulbright Fellowship, the Rolf D. Buhler Memorial Award, the William F. Ballhaus Prize, and the Hans G. Hornung Prize.

1986.summary: Seminar Speaker: CliMAS Graduate Student, Eddie Wolff
1986.description: Looking Aloft: The Roles and Environmental Controls of QLCS Updraft CoresQuasi-linear convective system (QLCS) tornadoes have long presented a challenge to forecasters due to their large spatial scale and relatively short-lived vortices, leading to shorter warning lead times relative to supercells. While common approaches to QLCS tornado prediction emphasize analysis of the lowest levels, this is often impossible due to limited radar coverage. However, there may also be utility in examining mid-tropospheric features of QLCSs, namely discrete updraft cores that arise from slabular lifting near the surface. These cores may be useful in identifying locations within a QLCS that are primed for tornadogenesis due to enhanced near-surface lifting and vorticity generation. While the mechanisms behind these updraft cores remain poorly understood, observational analysis shows a correlation between their size and intensity and 5-10 km environmental wind shear. Using a simple analytic model, we hypothesize that the response of the linear dynamics contribution to perturbation pressure to increases in shear magnitude could represent a connection between 5-10 km shear and updraft cores, though other pathways likely exist.  To further explore this connection, we have produced a suite of 6 high-resolution (250 m grid-spacing) QLCS simulations using CM1. We independently vary 5-10 km shear via changes to hodograph length as well as CAPE via alterations to the mid-level lapse rate. Our results show that updraft cores tend to be stronger in more highly-sheared environments, though impacts on hydrometeor trajectories and resulting cold pool intensity present a complicating factor. The challenges of producing realistic QLCSs within an idealized model will also be discussed. https://illinois.zoom.us/j/87247933909?pwd=Yg9a5afZrUDAodWJBhap3HvxzMVVeo.1 Meeting ID: 872 4793 3909     Pass Code: 202496

1991.description: TITLE: Spectral properties of the logarithmic potential operator ABSTRACT: The classical Faber--Krahn inequality states that, among domains of given area, the ball minimizes the first Dirichlet eigenvalue of the Laplacian. We discuss an analogue for the logarithmic potential operator on $L^2(\Omega)$, \[\mathcal{L}u(x)=\int_\Omega \log\frac{1}{|x-y|}u(y)\,dy,\] where the planar domain $\Omega$ is bounded and open. Here the situation is reversed: symmetrization increases the largest eigenvalue. Assuming the diameter of the domain is at most $1$, we establish reverse Faber--Krahn inequalities under polarization and Schwarz (symmetric decreasing) symmetrization. We also consider domains containing a hole, investigating how the largest eigenvalue varies as an obstacle is translated or rotated within the domain. Finally, we characterize the existence of a negative eigenvalue in terms of the logarithmic capacity (transfinite diameter) of the domain. This talk is based on joint work with T. V. Anoop.

2074.description: Bring your project and materials and learn some sewing tips as well as handicrafts (knitting/crochet)! This activity is provided by the International Hospitality Committee on the 1st and 3rd Tuesdays of each month. Please RSVP to Christina Myers if you plan to attend, ckmyers2@gmail.com.

2075.summary: Public Health Clinic in Orchard Downs - Women, Infants, and Children
2075.description: The Women, Infants, and Children (WIC) supplemental food program is excited to serve families in the apartments in Family & Graduate Housing. Visit them every Thursday from 8:30 a.m.–12 p.m. and 1–4:30 p.m. at 2040-A Orchard Street to learn more or enroll during open hours. WIC provides vital support for families, including access to healthy foods, nutrition education, and resources for women and young children. If you have questions or prefer to schedule an appointment, call the main office at 217-531-4529 or 217-531-4307 (Spanish), Monday through Friday. Take advantage of this valuable program and help your family thrive!

2076.description: Join us at the Orchard Downs Community Center for Mother Goose on the Loose, featuring stories, music, dancing, and a free book for each child.  Caregivers of children ages 0-5 are also invited to Parent Connections to connect with other families and learn about developmental milestones.  Have an December birthday? Email Miss Hannah to arrange a special birthday celebration following Mother Goose!

2077.description: Looking for small kitchen items during your stay at Family & Graduate Housing? Stop by the Lending Storeroom every Saturday from 9–11 a.m. at 2044-A Orchard Downs (streetside entrance). Residents can borrow what they need for the duration of their stay—making life a little easier without extra expense. Have extra kitchen items to share? Donations are always welcome! Drop them off at the Storeroom during Saturday hours, or at the main Family & Graduate Housing office Monday–Friday between 8:30 a.m.–5 p.m. Interested in giving back? The Storeroom thrives thanks to volunteers. To join the team, contact Keach at keachs@yahoo.com.

2078.description: Residents are invited to participate in a free yoga class by Sri Sri Yoga every Sunday. Yoga offers numerous benefits for both the mind and body. It enhances flexibility, strength, and balance through various poses and stretches. 2079.description: Take a break from your studies and join us for wellness education, fun games, and other self-care stations! Goodie bag packing and notes of positivity, while supplies last. Food provided.

2080.description: It's one of our most popular traditions – Late Night Breakfast at ISR and IKE dining centers! Fuel up, de-stress, and have some fun before finals with University Housing's annual Late Night Breakfast, as meal plan holders can enjoy a free breakfast for a second dinner!

2081.summary: Dial-A-Carol: The fun begins – call in or volunteer!
2081.description: Since 1960, students, staff, and community volunteers in Snyder Hall have spread holiday cheer by singing seasonal favorites to callers from around the world through Dial-A-Carol. Beginning at 12:01 a.m. on Thursday, December 10, the Dial-A-Carol phone lines will open, and for the next seven days, University Housing residents and campus volunteers will take requests and sing callers’ favorite holiday tunes 24 hours a day. Anyone in need of a holiday pick-me-up can call 217-332-1882 anytime between 12:01 a.m. December 10 and 11:59 p.m. December 16. As the motto goes, “Give us a ring and hear us sing!” Interested in participating? Sign up online to sing to the world!
